en: Title: Acintyastava Author: Nāgārjuna Source: Tola & Dragonetti, 1985
In the language of India:
Acintyastava. In the language of Tibet: *bsam gyis mi khyab par bstod pa* (The Praise of the Inconceivable). Homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!
I bow to him who taught that things arising dependently lack intrinsic nature—he whose wisdom is peerless, inconceivable, and beyond illustration.
I prostrate to him who declared that all dependently arisen entities are devoid of intrinsic nature; to him whose wisdom is incomparable, inconceivable, and without parallel.
Just as you yourself have realized the selflessness of phenomena within the Mahāyāna, so too, out of the power of compassion, have you taught it to those possessed of intelligence.
(2) Just as you yourself have realized the selflessness of phenomena within the Mahāyāna, so too, out of the power of compassion, have you taught it to those possessed of intelligence. (2)
You have declared that what arises from conditions is unarisen;
since it is not born by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*), it is revealed as empty.
(3) That which arises dependently from conditions was taught by you to be unarisen; because it is not produced by way of its own-nature (*svabhāva*), it is thoroughly demonstrated as empty.
Just as an echo arises here in dependence upon sound,
and just as it is like an illusion or a mirage, so too does the arising of existence occur.
If illusions, mirages, cities of the Gandharvas, reflections, and dreams were unproduced, then their perception and so forth would not exist.
(5) If illusions, mirages, cities of the Gandharvas, reflections, and dreams were unproduced, then their seeing and so forth would be without a [corresponding] object. (5)
Just as these things are considered to be produced from causes and conditions,
so too, O Protector, you have taught that the entire universe, arising from conditions,
is conventional.
"All that is produced, whatever it may be, is merely the prattle of fools;
it resembles an empty fist, being revealed as something that does not correspond to reality.
(7) Whatever is spoken by the foolish is called "produced"; it exists like an empty fist, being demonstrated as not being according to the truth.
When a produced thing has not yet arisen, how could it be present?
Through the destruction of what would it become past? And what does that which is about to arise depend upon?
When a produced entity has not arisen, how could it be present? Through the destruction of what would it become past? Furthermore, how could that which is about to arise have any dependence?
An entity is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both;
it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent. At that time, how could anything else arise?
An entity is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent. At that time, how could anything else arise?
That which is unarisen has no intrinsic nature; how, then, could there be an arising from itself?
Since the non-existence of intrinsic nature is established, there is also no arising from another.

(10) That which is unarisen has no intrinsic nature; therefore, from what could it arise? Since the absence of an entity with intrinsic nature is established, there is no arising even from another. (10)
If self-nature exists, other-nature would exist; if other-nature exists, self-nature is asserted.
The establishment of these two is relative, as it has been taught to be like "this side" and "the far side.
If self-nature exists, other-nature would exist; if other-nature exists, self-nature would exist. These two are established as being dependent, as it was said, like "this side" and "the far side."
When nothing whatsoever is expected, then how could anything exist?
When length is not expected, then how could there be shortness and so forth?
(12) Non-existence exists only when existence exists; likewise, shortness exists only when length exists.
And since existence exists only when non-existence exists, therefore neither of the two is real.
(13) When there is nothing whatsoever upon which something depends, then what could arise from what? When there is no "long" upon which it depends, then how could "short" and so forth exist?
How could oneness and likewise multiplicity, the past and the future,
affliction and purification, or correctness and falsity exist by themselves? (14)
Just as there is no oneness and so forth, so it is with the past, the future, and so on; likewise for the afflictions. How could even the correct or the false arise from themselves?
For when no entity exists by its own nature, what could possibly exist at that time?
That which is called "other" does not exist without its own intrinsic nature.
(15) If an entity does not exist from itself, then at that time, what could all [others] be? What is it that is called "other"? It is not so if it lacks its own intrinsic nature. (15)
When there is neither intrinsic nature (svabhāva) nor extrinsic nature (parabhāva) of phenomena, then what dependent [grasping] could there be for one seized by the obsession of grasping at things?
When there is no extrinsic nature, then phenomena lack intrinsic nature; at that time, what purposeful vehicle could there be for one who grasps at extrinsic nature as a real thing?
From the very beginning they are equal, and by their very nature they are in nirvāṇa; they are unarisen in reality— therefore, all phenomena have been taught by you.
O wise one, you have revealed that form and the other aggregates are devoid of intrinsic nature;
they are like foam, bubbles, illusions, mirages, and plantain trees. (18)
If that which is perceived by the sense faculties were to exist in reality, then children would be knowers of reality; what then would be the use of the knowledge of reality?
(19) If that which is perceived by the sense faculties were to exist in reality, then children would be knowers of reality; what then would be the use of the knowledge of reality? (19)
You have stated that the sense faculties are insentient, lack the nature of valid cognition, are indeterminate, and involve a distorted comprehension.
"Having realized exactly as it is that by which the world is not understood as it truly is, you have declared that the world is obscured by ignorance.
(21) "Because [the world] does not realize what is, having understood it exactly as it is, you have therefore said that the world is obscured by ignorance. (21)
"To say 'it exists' is the view of eternalism; to say 'it does not exist' is the view of nihilism.
Therefore, this Dharma has been taught by you as being free from these two extremes.
(22) "To say 'it exists' is the view of eternalism; to say 'it does not exist' is the view of nihilism. Therefore, this Dharma has been taught by you as being free from these two extremes. (22)
Therefore, you have taught that all phenomena are free from the four alternatives;
they are not even objects of consciousness, so how much less can they be the domain of words?
Just as the vision of two moons produced by a magician’s trick in a dream is neither a real thing nor an unreal thing, so too has the world been seen by you.
Just as one perceives things arising from dreams, magical illusions, or the vision of two moons and the like, so too have you seen that the emergence of the world is not a real occurrence.

Just as a son born in a dream is seen to exist and then perish, so too has the world been described by you as not truly born, existing, or perishing in reality. Just as an arising from a cause is seen in a dream, so it is with everything else.
The arising of all things is accepted as such, and their dissolution is likewise accepted.
Just as one perceives the occurrence [of things] from causes within a dream, so too is the arising of all entities; their destruction is held to be exactly like that.

Just as suffering arises from passion and the like, so too do affliction and cyclic existence; yet you have taught that liberation comes from the fulfillment of the accumulations, all being like a dream. (27)
Likewise, you have taught that attachment and the like, suffering, cyclic existence, all afflictions, the accumulation of merit, and even liberation are like a dream.
Likewise, that which is born and that which is unborn, that which has come and that which has gone, as well as the bound and the liberated—thus the wise one who knows reality does not desire duality.
(28) Just so, regarding the born and the unborn, the come and the gone, and likewise the bound and the liberated, the knower of reality does not accept these two. (28)

For that which has no arising at all, what nirvāṇa could there be? Since it is like the appearance of an illusory elephant, it is in reality primordially quiescent. (29) gang las skyes pa yod ma yin || de la mya ngan ’das gang yod || sgyu ma’i glang po ’dra ba’i phyir || don du gzhon nas zhi ba nyid ||

Just as a magical elephant is considered to be produced yet not produced, so too the entire universe is produced, yet in reality it is unproduced. (30) Even though it has arisen, it is unarisen, just like a magical elephant; likewise, the whole world has arisen, yet in truth it is unarisen. (30)

And those beings who enter nirvāṇa have not been born at all; it has been clearly stated by you, O Great Sage, that "no one has been liberated by anyone.
(32) "O Great Sage, because sentient beings are not born from themselves, for that reason you have clearly declared: 'No one whatsoever has been liberated by anyone. (32)

Just as that which is created by a magician is empty of intrinsic reality, so too is everything else; you have stated that the entire world is empty of intrinsic reality, and the agent is likewise. (33)
Even an agent, if created by another, does not escape being something that has been made;
or else, it follows that the agent would be the performer of its own action.
(34) The agent too, if made by another, Would become something that has been made. Alternatively, performing its own action, It would follow that it is [simultaneously] the agent. (34)
"You have proclaimed loudly that this entire world is mere name;

apart from the designation, no designated object exists. (35) "You have praised and declared that all these things are merely names; there is no referent to be expressed that exists as something other than the expression itself. (35)
On this basis, it has been revealed that all phenomena are mere conceptual construction;
yet even that conceptual construction is said to be non-existent, by which emptiness is conceptually constructed. (36)
Therefore, you have taught that all phenomena are mere conceptualization; you have also taught that even the conceptualization by which one conceives of emptiness does not exist.
It transcends the duality of existence and non-existence, yet it does not transcend anything whatsoever. It is neither cognition nor the object of cognition; it is neither non-existent nor existent.

(37) It transcends the duality of existence and non-existence, yet in some respects it does not transcend them. There is neither cognition nor the object of cognition; it is that which is neither non-existent nor existent. (37)
That which is neither one nor many, neither both nor neither;
it is without substrate, unmanifest, inconceivable, and incomparable.
(38) That which is neither one nor many, neither both nor nothing at all; it is without foundation, unmanifest, inconceivable, and beyond illustration. (38)
That which neither arises nor ceases, which is neither annihilated nor eternal, is like space; it is not within the domain of syllables or conceptual knowledge.
(39) Whatever is without arising and without cessation, without end and without permanence, that is like space; it is not the sphere of activity for letters or gnosis.
That which is dependent origination, that very thing you consider to be emptiness;

such is the true Dharma, and the Tathāgata is equal thereto. (40) That which is dependent origination, that very thing you maintain to be emptiness; the sublime Dharma is likewise, and the Tathāgata is identical to it. (40)
That reality is also accepted as the ultimate truth, suchness, and the substance;
it is real and non-deceptive, and one is called a Buddha because of the awakening to it. (41)
That is the meaning of reality, it is suchness, and it is held to be substantial; because it is non-deceptive and complete, it is called "Buddha."
Therefore, the Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings are in fact non-different;
by that [realization], you consider yourself and others to be equal. (42)
Emptiness is not other than things, nor do things exist without it;
therefore, you have revealed that dependently arisen things are empty.
(43) Emptiness is not other than things, nor do things exist without it; therefore, you have taught that dependently arisen things are empty. (43)
Conventional reality arises from causes and conditions and is dependent; it is therefore called "the dependent. Ultimate reality, however, is uncontrived.

Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*), reality (*tattva*), substance (*dravya*), entity (*vastu*), and existence (*sat*)—these do not exist as imagined (*parikalpita*); the dependent (*paratantra*) is likewise not found. (45)
Essential nature, intrinsic nature, and the existence of real entities as well; the non-existence of imagined things—these do not exist in the dependent nature.

You have declared that to say "it exists" regarding an imagined entity is superimposition (samāropa); and you have revealed that to say "it does not exist" because of the cessation of what was produced is nihilism (uccheda).

(46) You have stated that the assertion "the imagined entity exists" is a case of reification; and you have stated that the assertion "it does not exist because what was created has perished" is a case of annihilationism.
Through the knowledge of reality, neither annihilation nor permanence is asserted;
the entire world is held to be empty of intrinsic entity, resembling a mirage.
(47) Through the knowledge of reality, there is no annihilation, nor is permanence taught; the world is empty of substantiality, and for that reason, it is considered like a mirage.
Just as the water of a mirage is neither annihilated nor eternal, so too has the entire world been described as neither annihilated nor eternal.
(48) Just as the water of a mirage is neither annihilated nor eternal, so too has it been taught that all wandering beings are neither annihilated nor eternal. (48)

Just as the object of knowledge exists when there is knowledge, so too does knowledge exist when the object of knowledge exists.
When it is realized that both are unarisen, what then exists?

(50) Just as the object of knowledge exists because of the existence of knowledge, so too does that knowledge exist because of the existence of the object of knowledge. When both are realized to be unarisen, what then exists? (50)
Having thus clearly explained it through such analogies as that of an illusion, the supreme physician taught the True Dharma, which is the remedy for all views.
(51) Having thus clearly demonstrated it through such analogies as that of an illusion, the supreme physician taught the True Dharma, which brings about the cessation of all views. (51)
This is that supreme reality, the teaching on the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature;
it is the unsurpassed remedy for those seized by the demon of grasping at entities. (52)

This wonderful lion’s roar of selflessness has been uttered by you, which cuts through the fear of grasping at substantial entities and strikes terror into the deer-like followers of false teachers. (54)
You have uttered that marvelous lion’s roar of selflessness, which cuts through the fear of grasping at true existence and strikes terror into the deer of the non-Buddhists.
The drum of the Dharma, profound with the teaching of emptiness, has been struck;
the conch of the Dharma, with its great sound of the absence of intrinsic nature, has been blown. (55)
The great drum of the Dharma, most profound emptiness, has been struck; the great conch of the Dharma, the sound of the absence of intrinsic nature, has been blown.
The nectar of the Buddhas' teaching is declared to be the dowry of the Dharma;
it is pointed out as the definitive meaning (nītārtha), for it is indeed the very emptiness of all phenomena.
(56) The substance of the Dharma, the nectar of the Buddha's teaching, has been proclaimed; it is also taught as the definitive meaning, the very nature of all phenomena. (56)

Furthermore, O Protector, those teachings concerning arising and cessation, and so forth, as well as sentient beings, the life-principle, and so on— which you have spoken— are of interpretable meaning and are conventional reality.

He who has reached the absolute further shore of the ocean of the perfection of wisdom—he, rich in the jewels of meritorious qualities, has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of your qualities.

(58) He who has himself reached the further shore of the ocean of the perfection of wisdom—he, wealthy in the jewels of meritorious qualities, O Protector, has crossed to the further shore of your qualities. (58)
Having thus praised the Lord of the World, who is inconceivable and beyond illustration,

by whatever merit I have obtained, may the world become equal to you. (59) By this praise of the inconceivable and peerless Lord of the World, whatever merit I have acquired, through that may all beings become equal to you.
The *Acintyastava* (Praise of the Inconceivable), composed by the great master Nāgārjuna, is hereby completed.
